text.title: django-imports Core Rules
text.summary: Eleven testable rules for import discipline in a multi-app Django repo: section order, aliasing, and the ordered ladder of circular-import strategies.

rule.statement: Imports are grouped in this order, one blank line between groups: (1) `__future__`, (2) standard library, (3) third-party (Django, DRF, Celery), (4) first-party absolute (`apps.*`, `core.*`, `config.*`), (5) local relative. Nobody sorts by hand — `ruff check --select I --fix` does it.
rule.rationale: PEP 8 fixes the first three groups; Django projects need the fourth to make the cross-app dependency graph visible at a glance. Hand-sorting produces noisy diffs that reviewers learn to skip, which is how the convention dies.

rule.statement: Django core, third-party packages and every cross-app reference use absolute imports. Within one app, single-dot relative imports are correct and preferred: `from .models import User`.
rule.rationale: An absolute path tells the reader which app a name comes from without opening another file. Inside one app there is no ambiguity — only one `User` is in scope — so the single-dot form is both shorter and survives the app being renamed.

rule.statement: Multi-dot relative imports (`from ..`, `from ...`) are forbidden. Replace with the absolute `apps.<app>.<module>` path.
rule.rationale: A multi-dot import encodes the physical directory depth. Moving `apps/users/` under `apps/accounts/users/` breaks every `from ...users.models import` in the repo at once, and the failure is an ImportError at startup, not a test failure.

rule.statement: Every cross-app import uses a module alias: `from apps.users import models as user_models`, referenced as `user_models.User`. Direct symbol imports across apps (`from apps.users.models import User`) are forbidden even when no collision exists today.

rationale.source: internal lint rule; circular-import incident history

rule.rationale: Two apps eventually both export `User`, `Status` or `Profile`; the second import silently shadows the first and the bug only fires when both code paths run. Aliasing also imports the module rather than the symbol, which is what lets Django finish loading the app registry before the name is resolved.

rule.statement: Resolve a circular import by climbing this ladder in order, never skipping upward: (1) string FK reference, (2) `apps.get_model()` for runtime model access in a service, (3) a `TYPE_CHECKING` guard for type-only imports, (4) a function-scoped import as a last resort, (5) extraction into `core/` when more than one of the above is needed in the same module.
rule.rationale: Each rung costs more than the one above it. String references are free and idiomatic; `apps.get_model()` is safe but verbose; a `TYPE_CHECKING` guard breaks runtime `isinstance`; a function-scoped import pays on every call. Reaching for rung 4 first hides a structural problem that rung 5 is the actual fix for.

rule.statement: `ForeignKey` and `ManyToManyField` targets are written as strings: `ForeignKey("users.User", on_delete=...)`, never `ForeignKey(User, ...)`, for every cross-app relation.
rule.rationale: A string reference is resolved by the app registry after every app has loaded, so it carries no load-order dependency. A class reference forces `users` to be importable while `billing` is still being imported, which fails or succeeds depending on `INSTALLED_APPS` order.

rule.statement: A service or selector that needs a model class at runtime but cannot import it at module level uses `apps.get_model("users", "User")` inside the function body.
rule.rationale: `get_model` reads the fully populated registry, moving the resolution from import time to call time. That breaks the cycle without hard-coding an import path, so the module keeps working if the model later moves.

rule.statement: Imports used only in annotations live inside `if TYPE_CHECKING:`, paired with `from __future__ import annotations` — EXCEPT in `apps/*/serializers.py`, where DRF and drf-spectacular need real types at runtime. Enforced by ruff's `TCH` rules.

rationale.source: PEP 563 + ruff TCH + drf-spectacular issue history

rule.rationale: `TYPE_CHECKING` is False at runtime, so the import never executes and the cycle disappears while mypy and pyright still see it. DRF is the documented exception: `get_type_hints()` on a stringified ForwardRef raises at serializer construction time.

rule.statement: When three or more apps depend on each other cyclically, extract the shared types, constants or base classes into a `core/` (or `common/`) app. `core/` imports from no other app — ever.
rule.rationale: A cycle across three apps is a shared concept without a home. Giving it one establishes a direction — every app may import `core/`, `core/` imports nobody — which resolves the whole cluster in one change instead of patching each edge.

rule.statement: Configure ruff with `known-first-party = ["apps", "config", "core"]` and an explicit `section-order`. Run `ruff check --select I --fix` on staged files in pre-commit.
rule.rationale: Without `known-first-party`, ruff files `apps.users` under third-party and merges it with the Django imports, so the cross-app dependencies become invisible in the diff. A misconfigured first-party list is why "the import order rule" quietly stops being enforced.

rule.statement: `from anywhere import *` is forbidden in every module, including `__init__.py` and settings splits.
rule.rationale: A star import binds an unknown set of names, so neither a reader nor ruff can tell what is in scope or which names are unused. It also leaks any public name the source module happened to import itself.
